title: Europe's Ancient Forests Were Nothing Like We Imagined
summary:
Picture the wilderness of central Europe 100,000 years ago, or even a million years ago. You might imagine an endless expanse of towering trees, with thick canopies blocking sunlight from reaching the ground. But according to a major new study, that familiar image of Europe's ancient forests is probably misleading.

Instead, much of the continent was a vibrant landscape of scattered trees, open woodlands, grassy clearings, and colorful wildflower meadows. Birds and butterflies flourished in these sunlit habitats, while enormous grazing animals helped prevent trees and shrubs from taking over.

Researchers led by Aarhus University have found that this mixture of habitats dominated Europe's landscapes for more than 20 million years. Far from being the continent's original natural condition, the dense, dark forests common in many parts of Europe today appear to be a relatively recent development in its ecological history.

Published in the journal Biological Conservation, the findings challenge a longstanding assumption about what Europe's wilderness looked like before widespread human intervention. They also raise important questions about modern reforestation programs, which often prioritize planting dense forests to combat climate change and protect biodiversity.

"The study shows that current reforestation practices are on the wrong track — both here in Denmark, where subsidies are only granted for planting dense forests, and elsewhere in Europe. This will not only be harmful for biodiversity; it will be in direct contradiction to the type of ecosystems that Europe's species have evolved in over millions of years," says Professor Jens-Christian Svenning of Aarhus University, senior author of the study.

For decades, conservation strategies have been influenced by the "closed-forest paradigm." This is the belief that dense forests with nearly continuous tree canopies were Europe's natural landscape before humans began clearing land for agriculture and settlements. Under this view, restoring nature often means allowing trees to reclaim open areas or planting forests where they no longer exist.

The new research suggests that this approach may overlook a crucial part of Europe's ecological history. Rather than being uniformly covered by dense forests, the continent was characterized by changing combinations of grasslands, shrubs, and woodlands with different amounts of tree cover. These landscapes supported a rich variety of species adapted to both wooded and open environments. Large plant-eating animals also played a major role in maintaining this diversity by grazing, browsing, and disturbing vegetation.

To reconstruct Europe's ancient environments, the researchers examined an unusually extensive collection of evidence spanning millions of years. Previous studies have generally concentrated on more recent periods. This investigation extended much further into the past, examining paleoecological records from the Miocene epoch, which began around 23 million years ago, through the pre-industrial era. Paleoecology is the study of ancient ecosystems using clues preserved in fossils, sediments, and other natural records. Because no single type of evidence can provide a complete picture of the distant past, the team combined several independent methods.
why_it_matters: If Europe's wildlife evolved in open, sunlit landscapes, planting only dense forests could harm the very species conservation aims to protect, so the study pushes tree-planting programs to rethink their approach.

questions.question: What did ancient Europe look like, according to the new study?
options: Only tall mountains and bare rock
Open woodlands, grassy clearings, and wildflower meadows
Endless dense, dark forest
A frozen desert with no plants
questions.correct_answer: Open woodlands, grassy clearings, and wildflower meadows

options: About 1,000 years
About 100,000 years
About 200 years
More than 20 million years

questions.question: What is the "closed-forest paradigm"?
options: The idea that forests should never be studied
A plan to plant trees on every farm in Denmark
A rule that forbids cutting down any tree in Europe
The belief that dense forests were Europe's natural landscape before humans cleared land
questions.correct_answer: The belief that dense forests were Europe's natural landscape before humans cleared land

background_read: Forests are not all alike: some are dense, with tree tops joining into a roof that shades the ground, while others are open woodlands where sunlight reaches grass and flowers below.
Large grazing animals shape such landscapes by eating young trees and shrubs, which stops the land from closing up into thick forest.
Reforestation means planting trees where forest has been lost, and it is often done to store carbon and give wildlife a home.
To learn what a landscape looked like long ago, scientists study ancient clues such as fossils and layers of soil and sediment, a field called paleoecology.
Article_Structure: LEAD: The familiar image of ancient Europe as endless dense forest is probably wrong — it was mostly open, sunny landscapes.
KEY EVENT: Aarhus University researchers found open woodlands, clearings, and meadows dominated Europe for more than 20 million years.
├─ WHO: Researchers led by Aarhus University, including senior author Professor Jens-Christian Svenning.
├─ WHAT: Scattered trees, grassy clearings, and wildflower meadows, kept open by large grazing animals.
├─ WHEN: Over more than 20 million years, from the Miocene epoch through the pre-industrial era.
├─ HOW: By combining several independent methods and paleoecological records from fossils and sediments.
└─ WHY IT MATTERS: Dense forests today look recent, and planting only dense forests may harm biodiversity.
EVIDENCE: Paleoecological records spanning millions of years, including the Miocene epoch, which began around 23 million years ago.
OPEN QUESTION: How reforestation programs should change to match the open landscapes Europe's species evolved in.
